definition: Vituperate means to berate; to attack with harsh, abusive language.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vituperate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vituperate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Cicero could vituperate with the best of Rome, flaying a rival for an hour while the galleries took notes.
Criticize is far milder than vituperate — it can be fair, careful, even kind.
Lambaste stops just short of vituperate: a lambasting is a hard public thrashing, but vituperation settles into sustained, naked abuse.

To revile is to heap open scorn on someone — loud contempt, name-calling, public hatred. To vituperate is scorn made marathon: sustained, abusive language that batters on and on. A crowd can revile a referee in a single roar; vituperation needs paragraphs.

To castigate is to punish with words — a severe, formal censure aimed at a fault and meant to correct it. To vituperate abandons correction entirely: sustained abuse with only the target at its center and no lesson attached. Castigation wants improvement; vituperation only wants to wound.

In 1843, two rival balloonists -- Aldous Pike and the self-styled 'Professor' Merriweather -- turned the town's two newspapers into artillery.
Merriweather struck first with a paragraph mocking Pike's leaky silk.
Pike answered with six columns, and from then on he did not argue so much as vituperate.
Week after week his letters called Merriweather a fraud, a coward, a 'gasbag in trousers,' and worse; readers noted that Pike never once addressed the actual question of whose balloon flew higher.
The editor loved it -- circulation doubled -- but historians looking for technical substance find none: no data, no correction, no aim beyond the wound.
When Merriweather finally quit the town, Pike's letters simply stopped.
There had never been an argument to win, only a man to batter.
